fixes.explanation: The other spies don't fit here. The men who brought out the bad report were struck down by a plague before the LORD (Numbers 14:37). In verse 31, the LORD names the people's children as the ones He will bring in. Those are the same children the people had said would become plunder.

Yes, baker. "Of those men who had gone to spy out the land, only Joshua son of Nun and Caleb son of Jephunneh remained alive." (Numbers 14:38). The other men who brought out the bad report were struck down by a plague before the LORD (Numbers 14:37). Joshua and Caleb were among the spies, and they are the two who told the congregation the land was exceedingly good (Numbers 14:6-7).

That's a thoughtful guess, but the text doesn't say that. The plague comes just before, but burying the men is never mentioned. The people head up toward the ridge of the hill country, saying, "We have indeed sinned," they said, "but we will go to the place the LORD has promised." (Numbers 14:40). That is the plan the text gives.

That's it, baker. The whole congregation says, "If only we had died in the land of Egypt…" (Numbers 14:2). They add a second wish, that they had died in this wilderness. The text says the people wept that night (Numbers 14:1), and I think that's a lot of hurt and fear coming out all at once.

The people really do say this. Numbers 14:3 has them asking, "Why is the LORD bringing us into this land to fall by the sword?" So the statement is true. They say it to Moses and Aaron, and they put the blame on the LORD for bringing them in.

You got it, baker. They say, "Let us appoint a leader and return to Egypt." (Numbers 14:4). They say it to one another, so this plan is coming from the people talking among themselves. I think that shows how scared they were, since the plan ends with going back to Egypt.

Close, since the spies' report is what got the congregation grumbling (Numbers 14:36). But the people don't ask for a new scout. They say, "Let us appoint a leader and return to Egypt." (Numbers 14:4). The word is leader, and the plan is heading back to Egypt.

Dangerous sounds like a bad report, but it isn't what Joshua and Caleb say. They were among those who had spied out the land (Numbers 14:6). They tell the whole congregation, "The land we passed through and explored is an exceedingly good land." (Numbers 14:7). Their word is good.

Moses and Aaron are the leaders the people were grumbling against, so it's a fair guess. But Joshua and Caleb don't name them as the ones who will bring Israel in. They say, "If the LORD delights in us, He will bring us into this land, a land flowing with milk and honey, and He will give it to us." (Numbers 14:8). The "He" there is the LORD.

Yes, that's what happens. "But the whole congregation threatened to stone Joshua and Caleb." (Numbers 14:10). That's how the congregation answers two men who just told them the land was good. I think this one hurts. Then the glory of the LORD appears to all the Israelites at the Tent of Meeting.

That's the word, baker. The LORD says to Moses, "…How long will they refuse to believe in Me, despite all the signs I have performed among them?" (Numbers 14:11). The signs had been performed among them, and still they refused to believe. The LORD puts the question to Moses as a how-long.

Rejoice is a happy word, and this isn't a happy moment. The LORD asks how long they will refuse to believe in Him, despite all the signs He has performed among them (Numbers 14:11). I'd happily rejoice every time a batch comes out clean, friend, but that's my kitchen and not this verse. The missing word here is believe.

You've got it. The LORD says, "…I will do to you exactly as I heard you say." (Numbers 14:28). Just before that, He says He has heard the complaints the Israelites are making against Him (Numbers 14:27). Moses and Aaron are told what to say to the people, and later the text says Moses relayed these words to all the Israelites (Numbers 14:39).

That's right. The LORD says, "Your bodies will fall in this wilderness—all who were numbered in the census, everyone twenty years of age or older—because you have grumbled against Me." (Numbers 14:29). So it's far more than the spies. It reaches everybody counted who was twenty or older, with two exceptions the LORD names: Caleb and Joshua (Numbers 14:30).

Servants never show up in this verse. The LORD says, "But I will bring your children, whom you said would become plunder, into the land you have rejected—and they will enjoy it." (Numbers 14:31). The people had said their children would become plunder (Numbers 14:3), and He says those children are the ones He will bring in. So the answer is the children themselves.

That's what they say. "We have indeed sinned," they said, "but we will go to the place the LORD has promised." (Numbers 14:40). They got up early the next morning to do it. The LORD had told them to turn back and head for the wilderness (Numbers 14:25), so this goes the other way.

Not this time. The text says they went up "…though neither Moses nor the ark of the covenant of the LORD moved from the camp." (Numbers 14:44). Moses had warned them, "Do not go up, lest you be struck down by your enemies, because the LORD is not among you." (Numbers 14:42). That warning was about the LORD not being among them, and the text separately tells us Moses and the ark stayed in the camp.
